title: How does sand turn into rock? Quiz
description: After watching the episode on how loose sand becomes rock you can't break, do you know what glues the grains together?

questions.question: How do we know the Machinchang rocks were once sand?
options: Because they're soft and crumble in your hand
Because you can see the grains, and the rocks still carry ripple marks like today's beaches and traces of ancient creatures
questions.explanation: The rocks kept their own evidence: up close you can see the grains, the surfaces show ripples just like the ones on a beach today, and some still have the tracks and burrows of ancient animals. Over 500 million years ago, this was a great stretch of sand left by rivers and the sea.

questions.question: You squeeze a handful of dry sand hard. What happens when you let go?
options: It's turned into a small rock
questions.explanation: Squeezing pushes the grains closer together, but nothing holds them, so they fall apart as soon as you open your hand. Add a little water and the sand holds its shape, but water is only a temporary glue: a sandcastle still collapses once it dries.

questions.question: Where does the "glue" that turns sand into rock come from?
options: Minerals that groundwater leaves between the grains, such as calcium carbonate
Salt left behind when seawater dries
The grains are squeezed so hard that they melt together
questions.explanation: Buried sand sits soaked in groundwater. Minerals dissolved in the water slowly come out and grow into tiny crystals between the grains, locking them together. In a lot of sandstone the glue is calcium carbonate, the same stuff as the limescale in a kettle.

questions.question: Limescale builds up in a kettle quite quickly. Why does the glue underground take so long?
options: Because limescale appears fast only because the water is boiled; nobody boils anything underground, so the glue grows slowly, kilometres down
Because the minerals underground are completely different from limescale
questions.explanation: A kettle keeps heating the water, so the minerals come out fast. The glue between the grains forms several kilometres down and only grows slowly, over a very long time.

questions.question: Why hasn't the sand we walk on at the beach usually turned to rock?
options: Because beach sand is too fine
Because the waves keep moving it around, so it never gets buried and squeezed, and the glue never has time to grow
questions.explanation: Sand has to be buried and squeezed first, then wait for groundwater to leave its glue, which often takes millions of years. There are exceptions, though: on some tropical beaches sand can be cemented into beachrock within a few decades.
